title: Rome's intellect-only subject is of absolute faith; living formed faith occupies will too
source_text: XXVII. Porro quum dicunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae subjectum fidei non esse voluntatem, sed intellectum solum, id proculdubio intelligendum est de fide absolute & in se considerata. Nam si sermo sit de fide viva, & per dilectionem operante, quam formatam appellant, dubitari non potest, quin illa, etiam ex eorum mente, non intellectum tantum, sed voluntatem etiam occupet, & in ea sedem habeat: quandoquidem includit, ipsis agnoscentibus, fiduciam & dilectionem, qui actus a voluntate non imperantur tantum, sed eliciuntur quoque: ac proinde in ista facultate, tanquam in subjecto proprio recipiuntur.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover when the Doctors of the Roman Church say faith's subject is not the will but intellect alone, that is without doubt to be understood of faith absolutely and considered in itself. For if the speech is of living faith working through love, which they call formed, it cannot be doubted that even on their mind it occupies not intellect only but also the will and has its seat there: since it includes, as they themselves acknowledge, trust and love, which acts are not only commanded by the will but also elicited by it: and therefore are received in that faculty as in their proper subject.
pass_b_english: Rome's intellect-only claim covers absolute faith in itself.
Living formed faith, even for them, seats trust and love in the will as elicited acts.

lemmas.gloss: faith absolutely and considered in itself

choices.why: Produced by the will, not only commanded.
